overview: Han-Zhao was a Southern Xiongnu-led state of northern China, historically dated 304-329. Its later phase is called Former Zhao. It was separate from the earlier Han dynasty and from rival Later Zhao. The imported map spans 300-400 and places a simplified outline well north of Chang’an and Luoyang, cities crucial to this story. It is not a reliable picture of the state’s full territory or lifetime.

periods.title: Liu Yuan’s foundation
periods.summary: Liu Yuan takes the title king of Han in 304 and emperor in 308.

periods.title: Conquest under Liu Cong
periods.summary: Han forces capture Luoyang in 311; Chang’an falls in 316, ending Western Jin.

periods.title: Liu Yao and Former Zhao
periods.summary: Following a succession crisis, Liu Yao takes power. In 319 he establishes his capital at Chang’an and changes the name to Zhao.

sections.title: A new state in a divided north

items.text: The Southern Xiongnu had already lived under Jin authority before Liu Yuan’s revolt. During the Jin princes’ civil wars, his aristocratic supporters built a government of their own. Their rise belonged to a world of settled communities, armies and competing courts, rather than a sudden arrival from outside China.

Calling the state Han was a political choice. Liu Yuan invoked an admired earlier dynasty; the later name Zhao recalled another prestigious historical name. Historian Wu Honglin studies these names as statements about rulers’ identities and claims to authority. A familiar name did not make this the old Han empire reborn.

Han-Zhao’s victories reshaped China. Its forces captured Luoyang in 311 and Chang’an in 316, taking Jin emperors prisoner. These were destructive conquests: the siege of Chang’an caused severe hunger. Winning a capital could make a ruler powerful while making the lives of the city’s families much harder.

Liu Yao had been orphaned and raised by Liu Yuan. This family relationship mattered politically as well as personally. Hu Hong emphasizes adoption when explaining Liu Yao’s position within the ruling house; uncertain details of distant ancestry should not obscure the practical importance of being brought up in that household.

After turmoil in 318, Liu Yao established his court at Chang’an and adopted the name Zhao in 319. Shi Le, formerly part of the same military coalition, established a rival Zhao regime. Historians distinguish Former Zhao from Later Zhao: the two governments eventually became enemies.

Ruling meant more than commanding cavalry. Han-Zhao established official posts and supported agriculture. Its rulers adopted Chinese governmental and literary practices while retaining connections to Xiongnu leadership. Fields and administrators helped sustain the court and its soldiers.

At Xiangjisi village near Xi’an, archaeologists excavated a tomb called M7 containing a pottery stove, well, mill, dishes and a spoon. It dates broadly from late Western Jin through Former or Later Zhao. These objects offer a nearby household comparison; its exact ruling dynasty remains uncertain.

The same tomb included pottery chickens, a pig, a dog and a male attendant. Cooking, animals and service were important enough to represent in burial. A miniature kitchen can be an archaeological treasure, even without a miniature chef. The objects express burial choices, rather than proving every home looked alike.

Chemical clues in bones can reveal meals that vanished long ago. A study of 25 people buried in the wider Guanzhong region during the Sixteen Kingdoms period found a diet dominated by millet, with some other plant foods or animals fed on them. This broader regional sample cannot provide a separate menu for Han-Zhao alone.

The Book of Jin reports strict rules under Liu Yao: embroidered silk clothing depended on official rank, drinking was permitted after late-autumn farm work, and cattle slaughter was restricted to certain sacrifices. These were royal commands, with harsh penalties, rather than a diary of what everyone actually did.

When Liu Yao was wounded and captured, his enemy assigned a doctor named Li Yong to treat him. The history identifies Li as a specialist in wounds and says he accompanied the injured ruler in a carriage. This records care for one important prisoner, not a general hospital system.

Liu Yao established schools near Chang’an’s palaces. The historical account describes selecting 1,500 students aged 13 to 25 and recruiting learned teachers. Successful students could receive court appointments. These were selective institutions preparing people for service, not schools attended by every child.

Liu Cong was remembered as a writer as well as a ruler, with more than a hundred poems and dozens of other compositions. Those works are now lost. A royal author could have plenty of readers in his lifetime and still leave no surviving collection for today’s children to open.

A song praised the defeated commander Chen An for caring for his soldiers. According to the transmitted history, Liu Yao admired it and ordered his court musicians to perform it, even though Chen An had been an opponent. Music could preserve affection for someone whom the victorious government had fought.

A reported discovery in 321 became a political argument: a piece of white jade supposedly carried a prophecy. Courtiers debated whether it promised victory or warned of danger. Historian Dong Gang examines the wordplay and political purposes of the story. This is a report in historical texts, not a surviving excavated message authenticated here.

A later history preserves Liu Yao’s message to his heir after his capture in 329: 勿以吾易意也, modern Mandarin wù yǐ wú yì yì yě, translated here as “Do not change your resolve on my account.” This is Chinese in modern type from the seventh-century Book of Jin. It is not his surviving original letter or an example of a separate Xiongnu script.

Much of this state’s history reached us through later compilations. Cui Hong’s early history of the Sixteen Kingdoms was used by subsequent historians, but its original text was eventually lost. Scholars compare surviving quotations and reconstructions, which helps explain why an apparently detailed story can still require careful checking.

ending.text: Later Zhao conquered the remaining Han-Zhao regime in 329 after capturing Liu Yao. Its rulers’ defeat did not erase the region’s communities. The map’s 400 endpoint is only imported coverage.
